content.intro: This lesson focuses on scheduled workflows. Scheduled workflows use cron expressions in UTC and are best for periodic checks or reports, not precise real-time scheduling guarantees. content_blocks.title: Core idea

content_blocks.code:
name: Scheduled health check
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 6 * * 1-5"
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  report:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Scheduled check executed at UTC schedule"
content_blocks.expected_output: GitHub schedules the workflow for 06:17 UTC Monday through Friday; actual start time may vary.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Validate the cron expression and UTC conversion before enabling the workflow on the default branch.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Change or remove the schedule after the maintenance use case ends.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain scheduled workflows, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose triggers and filters that run the right validation at the right time without exposing privileged jobs.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Scheduled workflows use cron expressions in UTC and are best for periodic checks or reports, not precise real-time scheduling guarantees. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
